summary:
Mission Control: Beyond Earth is an interactive educational game built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Players act as Mission Director, designing spacecraft, managing limited resources and flying complete missions across the solar system. Instead of answering trivia, they learn real aerospace engineering through trade-offs. A bigger engine adds thrust but also mass and fuel use, and more instruments mean more research but a heavier power draw.

The game offers 15 missions, from lunar orbit to deep space, and a 54-component equipment catalogue across ten categories. Each mission runs through an eight-stage simulation, from launch to evaluation, with dynamic events that force meaningful decisions. A 1,000-point scoring system rewards engineering quality and resource efficiency as well as success. Other features include a four-player cooperative LAN multiplayer mode, procedural sound, five ranks, twelve achievements and a Learn Basics section covering fifteen core concepts.

The spacecraft built in the Design Lab is the same one that launches and flies. Missions are deterministic and reproducible. Every event and failure comes with an educational explanation, and the mission report suggests how to improve the design.

The game was built with Next.js, React and TypeScript, runs entirely in the browser, and is released under the Apache License 2.0.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Mission Control: Beyond Earth is an interactive educational space mission design and simulation game. The player takes the role of a Mission Director who designs spacecraft, manages limited resources, and flies complete missions across the solar system.

The game follows a six-phase loop: PLAN → DESIGN → VALIDATE → LAUNCH → MANAGE → EVALUATE

  1. Plan — The player selects from 15 missions spanning the Moon, Mars, Venus, Mercury, the Sun, Europa, Saturn, Titan, asteroids, comets, and interstellar space. Each mission has a unique destination, difficulty, budget, mass limit, and environmental constraints.
  2. Design — The player builds a spacecraft from a 54-component catalogue across 10 categories (Propulsion, Fuel, Power, Communication, Science, Navigation, Thermal, Protection, Landing, Structure). A live SVG visualizer assembles the rocket in real-time as components are added — engines at the bottom, fuel tanks stacked above with interstage adapters, solar wings extending horizontally, instruments and antennas on top.
  3. Validate — The game runs a readiness check: budget, mass, power balance, fuel adequacy, required equipment, radiation shielding, thermal protection, and landing capability. Errors block launch; warnings are risks the player accepts.
  4. Launch — An 8-stage simulation begins: Launch (countdown, ignition, ascent with live telemetry), Separation (booster drift, solar wing deployment), Cruise, Navigation (trajectory correction burns), Arrival (orbital insertion or atmospheric entry with powered descent), Science (instrument scanning), Communication (data downlink to Earth), and Evaluation.
  5. Manage — During flight, 66 dynamic events trigger based on the spacecraft's design margins — solar storms, power faults, asteroid encounters, communication losses, fuel emergencies, discoveries. Each event presents 2-3 choices with real numeric consequences (fuel costs, science gains, reliability damage).
  6. Evaluate — The mission is scored out of 1,000 points across 5 categories: primary objectives (400), secondary objectives (150), engineering quality (200), resource efficiency (150), and decision-making (100). A full report provides strengths, weaknesses, recommendations, and educational notes.

The game also features 4-player cooperative LAN multiplayer with four distinct crew roles (Mission Commander, Chief Engineer, Navigation & Flight Director, Science & Comms Officer), a host-authoritative WebSocket server, reconnection tokens, and host migration.

What benefits does it have?

  • Educational depth — Players learn real aerospace engineering: propulsion trade-offs (chemical vs. ion), the rocket equation, solar derating by distance, radiation shielding, orbital mechanics, thermal protection, and communication link budgets. A Learn Basics reference section covers 15 fundamental topics from "What is a spacecraft?" to "What are exoplanets?"
  • No single correct answer — Multiple viable spacecraft configurations exist for every mission. The scoring system rewards engineering quality and resource efficiency, not just mission success, encouraging iterative improvement.
  • Deterministic and reproducible — The game engine is pure TypeScript with no I/O or hidden state. The same seed, spacecraft, and decisions always produce the identical flight, making every mission testable and reproducible.
  • Accessible — Runs entirely in a web browser with no installation required. Beginner-friendly language throughout, with a difficulty ladder from Beginner to Expert plus a Custom Challenge mode with 12 random constraints.
  • Player progression — Five ranks (Rookie Astronaut to Senior Mission Director) and twelve achievements reward continued learning and mission completion.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The project makes space mission engineering — one of humanity's most complex endeavors — accessible to students and the general public. A person with no aerospace background can sit down, pick a lunar mission, and within minutes be wrestling with the same trade-offs real mission planners face: mass vs. capability, fuel vs. delta-v, power generation vs. consumption, cost vs. reliability.

By presenting these trade-offs through interactive decision-making rather than memorization, the game builds intuition for how engineering systems interact. Players learn that successful space missions require balancing limited resources, understanding scientific requirements, anticipating problems, and making informed decisions under pressure — not simply selecting the most powerful equipment.

The game references 11 real NASA missions in its educational content (Perseverance, Juno, Cassini, Parker Solar Probe, Europa Clipper, OSIRIS-REx, Hubble, James Webb, Solar Orbiter, Voyager, and the Deep Space Network), grounding the gameplay in real space exploration history.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Framework: Next.js 16 (App Router) with React 19
  • Language: TypeScript 5 (strict mode) — all 100 source files are typed
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS 4 + shadcn/ui component library + Radix UI primitives
  • Animation: framer-motion for transitions and part assembly
  • Visuals: Pure SVG + CSS for all spacecraft models, flight scenes, and animations (no Three.js, no image sprites for simulations)
  • State management: Zustand 5 with persist middleware (localStorage)
  • Audio: Web Audio API — 15 procedurally synthesized sound cues, no audio files
  • Database: Prisma ORM + SQLite
  • Multiplayer server: Bun runtime with built-in WebSocket server (776 lines, host-authoritative)
  • Testing: Bun test — 5 test files, 1,286 lines covering engine logic, model sync, multiplayer, constraints, and PRNG determinism
  • Package manager/Runtime: Bun
  • Icons: lucide-react + Material Icons
  • Charts: Recharts (available for data visualization)

How is your project creative?

  • Shared spacecraft visual system — A single pure layout engine (model.ts) turns the live spacecraft configuration into ordered visual parts. The rocket you assemble in the Design Lab is the exact rocket that launches and flies — engine flames scale with throttle, wings unfold at separation, damage scorch persists for the rest of the flight. Interstage adapters automatically appear between fuel tanks of different diameters, just like real rockets.
  • Pure deterministic game engine — Approximately 5,000 lines of pure TypeScript with no I/O and no hidden state. The same modules run on both client and multiplayer server, so the simulation is never duplicated. Identical seed + spacecraft + decisions always produces the identical flight.
  • Procedural audio — All 15 sound cues (launch ignition, ascent rumble, engine burns, event alerts, touchdown thud, mission complete/failure stingers) are synthesized at runtime from oscillators, filtered noise, and envelopes. Zero audio files — the entire soundtrack is code.
  • Phased arrival scene — The arrival stage (stage 5) is a standalone component with multi-beat choreography: orbiters get approach → capture burn → orbit insertion → orbit trace; landers get approach → atmospheric entry → powered descent → touchdown. Destination-specific flourishes include Europa plumes, Titan haze, entry plasma for atmosphere-bearing bodies, and rough-landing tilt based on actual landing quality score.
  • 66 dynamic events with visual overlays — Events are classified into 11 types (storm, malfunction, comm loss, impact, asteroid, fuel emergency, discovery, panel deployment, advisory, eclipse), each with its own dynamic SVG overlay that reacts to the actual engine state.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Engineering realism vs. accessibility — The game uses simplified educational models rather than professional spacecraft engineering simulations, but every trade-off (mass vs. fuel, power generation vs. consumption, solar derating by distance) is grounded in real physics.
  • No single perfect solution — The design deliberately ensures multiple viable configurations per mission. The mission report recommends different refits depending on the player's weaknesses, so retrying with a different approach is always viable.
  • Difficulty progression — Five difficulty settings (Beginner through Custom Challenge) transform the real numbers: budget multipliers, mass limits, event rates, and 12 random constraints (budget cuts, mass limits, redundant comms requirements, banned equipment, extra science goals) that change the actual validation thresholds.
  • Accessibility and contrast — A full UI accessibility pass with contrast-audited buttons, focus rings, and prefers-reduced-motion support that disables all animations, leaving clean static scenes as fallback.
  • Multiplayer robustness — Host-authoritative server design (the server owns the official state; clients only send intents), reconnection tokens for dropped players, host migration when the host disconnects, and 15-minute room TTL for rejoins.
  • Open source — Released under Apache License 2.0, consistent with NASA Space Apps Challenge IP rules. All code, data, and artwork are freely available.
  • Persistent player progress — Spacecraft designs, mission logs (last 60 flights), sound preferences, and progression state (rank, achievements) persist in localStorage across sessions.
